title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Overview
Week 2 introduced a reproducible computational workflow. Week 3 asks a prior question:

What exactly are we measuring, and why should those measurements count as evidence for the question we care about?

Statistics begins long before a statistical test. It begins when researchers decide what counts as an observation, how an abstract idea becomes a variable, how that variable will be measured, which unit will be analyzed, and what research design can support the intended inference.
The lecture for this week follows one continuous argument:
concepts → definitions → variables → measurements → research design → inference
A strong analysis depends on alignment across that entire chain. Bernard and Wutich place variables, measurement, reliability, validity, units of analysis, causal logic, and research design at the foundation of social research (Bernard and Wutich 2027). Banning makes the same point from archaeology: convincing archaeological arguments require observations and measurements whose errors, biases, and inferential limits are understood (Banning 2020).






NoteThe Week 3 principle



A statistical result cannot be better than the concepts, measurements, and research design that produced the data.
Sophisticated analysis cannot rescue a variable that was badly defined, a measure that does not represent the intended concept, or a design that cannot answer the research question.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Questions

How does an abstract anthropological concept become an empirical variable?
What is the difference between a conceptual definition and an operational definition?
When is a variable unidimensional, and when does it require several indicators?
What makes a variable independent or dependent?
What are nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio levels of measurement?
Why should we preserve the highest useful level of information when collecting data?
How do reliability, precision, accuracy, and validity differ?
How can a measure be highly repeatable but still wrong?
What kinds of reliability and validity can researchers evaluate?
Why is real research iterative rather than perfectly linear?
What makes a research question feasible?
How do internal states, external states, reported behavior, observed behavior, and material traces differ as variables?
Why are qualitative and quantitative data not methodological opposites?
How can emic knowledge become measurable without losing its cultural grounding?
What makes a mixed-methods design coherent rather than merely “using several methods”?
What does research design contribute to causal inference?
Why does the unit of analysis matter?
What is the ecological fallacy?
How do observational/experimental, cross-sectional/longitudinal, and single-case/comparative decisions combine into eight basic designs?
How do participatory and action research change the relationship between researchers and participants?
What do reproducibility, metadata, provenance, and replicability add to research design in archaeology?

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Variables become evidence
Social research does not observe abstract ideas directly. Concepts such as social status, identity, wealth, mobility, political orientation, household organization, or cultural consonance must first be translated into observable properties.
A useful sequence is:

abstract concept → conceptual definition → operational definition → empirical values

Bernard and Wutich distinguish conceptual definitions from operational definitions: the first states what researchers mean by a concept; the second specifies the operations used to measure it (Bernard and Wutich 2027).
A variable is not identical to the concept. A variable is an empirical property that can take different values or categories.
For example:







Stage
Example




Abstract concept
household wealth


Conceptual definition
material and economic resources available to a household


Operational definition
record house area, storage capacity, durable goods, livestock holdings, and selected high-value objects using explicit coding rules


Empirical values
measured house area, counts, presence/absence codes, index values









ImportantOperational definitions are recipes



An operational definition should allow another researcher to understand how the data were generated.
That does not guarantee that the measure is good. It makes the measurement explicit enough to evaluate, criticize, reproduce, and improve.


This transparency is also central to computational reproducibility. Marwick argues that data and code provenance should expose the transformations that connect observations to published results (Marwick 2017). An operational definition does the same kind of work at the measurement stage.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Variables can be simple or multidimensional
text:
Variables can be simple or multidimensional
A unidimensional variable is represented primarily along one axis.
Examples include:

age;
height;
mass;
distance; and
counts.

A multidimensional variable has several analytically distinct facets.
Examples include:

wealth;
political orientation;
cultural consonance;
ethnic identity;
social status; and
household prosperity.

Bernard and Wutich use examples such as socioeconomic status to show why a single indicator may fail to capture a complex construct (Bernard and Wutich 2027).







Unidimensional
Multidimensional




often represented by one primary scale
contains several facets


a single indicator may sometimes be adequate
usually requires multiple indicators


easier to define operationally
requires explicit decisions about dimensions and weighting


example: length
example: socioeconomic status



Dimensionality therefore affects the measurement instrument. If the concept is multidimensional, asking one question or recording one attribute may give an incomplete or distorted measure.

Choose one concept from anthropology or archaeology—for example mobility, inequality, community integration, ritual investment, or household wealth.

Is it plausibly unidimensional or multidimensional?
What dimensions would you distinguish?
What observable indicators might represent each dimension?
What could be lost if you used only one indicator?

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Independent and dependent variables
Researchers often describe relationships using an independent variable (X) and dependent variable (Y).

Independent variable (X): presumed cause, explanatory variable, or predictor.
Dependent variable (Y): outcome, response, or effect.

But these roles are not intrinsic properties of variables. Theory assigns the roles.
For example, “education” might be treated as (X) when predicting income, but it might be treated as (Y) when studying how household resources influence educational attainment.
In an experiment, the researcher deliberately manipulates an independent variable. In observational research, researchers measure naturally occurring variation in (X) and examine whether it is associated with (Y) (Bernard and Wutich 2027).






NoteX and Y do not create causality by themselves



Calling one variable “independent” and another “dependent” does not prove a causal relationship. The labels express a theoretical model that must be evaluated with evidence and research design.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Bad theory can reverse causality
The lecture uses Bernard and Wutich’s Chicano high-school example to show how poor operationalization and poor causal theory can reinforce one another (Bernard and Wutich 2027).
Survey results had been interpreted as showing low career aspirations among Chicano students and insufficient parental encouragement. Ethnographic work revealed a different mechanism: parents often had high aspirations but also understood structural constraints, including the costs of higher education and discriminatory counseling. What looked like a deficit in parental aspiration was partly an artifact of how aspiration had been operationalized and how causality had been theorized.
The lesson is not simply “qualitative data are better.” The lesson is:

A measure can faithfully record answers to a badly framed question and still misrepresent the social mechanism.

Qualitative fieldwork improved the conceptual and operational definition. Those improved definitions could still be coded and analyzed quantitatively.
This is a crucial Week 3 point: measurement and theory cannot be separated.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Four levels
A variable’s level of measurement describes what information its values legitimately contain.









Level
What the values mean
Examples
What is defensible




Nominal
different named categories
site, artifact class, religion, raw-material type
equality/inequality, counts, proportions


Ordinal
ordered categories, but distances are not assumed equal
preservation rank, social-class rank, Likert responses
ordering plus nominal operations


Interval
equal intervals, but zero is not a true absence
Celsius, Fahrenheit, many standardized scores
differences and most arithmetic except meaningful ratios


Ratio
equal intervals and a meaningful zero
age, mass, counts, distance
full arithmetic, including ratios



Information content generally increases from nominal to ratio. The kinds of summaries and analyses that make sense depend partly on the level at which the variable was measured (Bernard and Wutich 2027; Banning 2020).






ImportantR storage type is not measurement level



R may store both a site code and a person’s name as character, while storing a nominal category coded 1, 2, 3 as numeric.
glimpse() tells you how R stores a column. It does not tell you the variable’s statistical measurement level.
Measurement level comes from the meaning of the values and the rules used to generate them.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Measure at the highest defensible level
text:
Measure at the highest defensible level
Higher-level information can often be collapsed downward.
For example:

age_demo <- tibble(
  exact_age = c(18, 23, 29, 34, 47, 62)
) |>
  mutate(
    age_band = cut(
      exact_age,
      breaks = c(0, 19, 29, 39, 49, 64, Inf),
      right = TRUE
    )
  )

age_demo

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  exact_age age_band
      <dbl> <fct>   
1        18 (0,19]  
2        23 (19,29] 
3        29 (19,29] 
4        34 (29,39] 
5        47 (39,49] 
6        62 (49,64] 


Exact ages can be converted into age brackets.
But once only the bracket is retained, the exact ages cannot be reconstructed.






NoteInformation loss is usually one-way



Exact age → age category is possible.
Age category → exact age is not.
When practical and ethical, collect data at the highest defensible level of detail and aggregate later for analysis.


This principle has an archaeological analogue. The BIAD Standards recommend preserving original, fine-grained chronological associations and raw observations even when researchers later aggregate phases for analysis (Reiter et al. 2024). Once distinct phases are published only as one broad period, later researchers cannot reliably recover the original detail.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Four different questions
The lecture distinguishes four dimensions of measurement quality:








Dimension
Core question
Typical problem




Reliability
Does the measurement repeat consistently?
random or observer-dependent variation


Precision
How fine is the resolution of the measurement?
coarse scale or instrument resolution


Accuracy
How close is the measurement to the relevant target or standard?
systematic bias


Validity
Does the measurement represent the intended concept?
wrong construct, proxy, or inference



These terms are related but not interchangeable (Bernard and Wutich 2027; Banning 2020).
A digital caliper can be precise but miscalibrated. Two analysts can agree perfectly on a coding rule that operationalizes the wrong concept. A laboratory measurement can be accurate for the chemical property measured but invalid as a proxy for the social process a researcher claims it represents.






ImportantStatistical sophistication cannot repair faulty measurement



A model can estimate relationships among the numbers you give it. It cannot determine whether those numbers validly represent the concept you intended to study.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Reliability and accuracy are not the same
text:
Reliability and accuracy are not the same
The following reproducible illustration adapts the logic of the lecture’s target diagram.

measurement_demo <- tribble(
  ~condition, ~x, ~y,
  "Unreliable + invalid",  1.1,  2.7,
  "Unreliable + invalid",  3.1,  1.1,
  "Unreliable + invalid",  1.8,  3.5,
  "Unreliable + invalid",  3.4,  2.6,
  "Unreliable + invalid",  2.2,  0.9,
  "Reliable but invalid",  2.0,  2.1,
  "Reliable but invalid",  2.2,  1.9,
  "Reliable but invalid",  1.9,  2.2,
  "Reliable but invalid",  2.1,  2.0,
  "Reliable but invalid",  2.0,  1.8,
  "Reliable + valid",      0.1,  0.1,
  "Reliable + valid",     -0.1,  0.2,
  "Reliable + valid",      0.2, -0.1,
  "Reliable + valid",     -0.2,  0.0,
  "Reliable + valid",      0.0, -0.2
)

ggplot(measurement_demo, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ condition) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1, 4), ylim = c(-1, 4)) +
  labs(
    x = "Horizontal deviation from target",
    y = "Vertical deviation from target"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Reliability and validity/accuracy are different properties. Tight clustering indicates repeatability; location relative to the target indicates whether the measurements are centered appropriately.





Figure 1 illustrates three possibilities:

Unreliable + invalid: readings vary widely and do not center on the target.
Reliable but invalid: readings repeat closely but cluster around the wrong place.
Reliable + valid: readings repeat closely and are centered appropriately.

Tight clustering alone is therefore not enough.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Reliability asks whether measurement repeats
Several forms of reliability answer different repeatability questions.







Reliability approach
Question




Interobserver / intercoder
Do different researchers measure or code the same case similarly?


Test–retest
Does the same instrument produce stable results when repeated under comparable conditions?


Parallel-form
Do equivalent versions of an instrument agree?


Internal consistency
Do items intended to measure one construct cohere?



A simple classical model is:
[ X = T + e ]
where:

(X) is the observed score;
(T) is the underlying true component; and
(e) is random measurement error.

The model is a way of thinking about observed values as a mixture of signal and error. It does not imply that every social or archaeological construct has a directly observable “true score.”

Reliability in archaeology
Interobserver reliability is especially important when analysts classify artifacts, skeletal traits, botanical remains, or images. Banning emphasizes that some observed variation can arise from differences among observers or instruments rather than from the archaeological objects themselves (Banning 2020).
Vaesen and Hussain add an important caution: replicability or inter-analyst agreement is not identical to reliability or interpretive value (Vaesen and Hussain 2026). Some archaeologically meaningful properties are genuinely ambiguous because of preservation, continuous variation, or differences in analytical traditions.






WarningDo not optimize measurement quality by measuring only what is easy



A variable can be easy to record consistently but weakly related to the archaeological question.
A difficult-to-code variable may still contain important behavioral information.
The goal is not maximum agreement at any cost. The goal is a defensible balance among reliability, validity, uncertainty, interpretive value, and feasibility.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Validity asks whether the intended concept is measured
text:
Validity asks whether the intended concept is measured
Four common forms of validity are:







Type
Main question




Face validity
Does the measure appear plausible on its face?


Content validity
Does it cover the important dimensions of the concept?


Construct validity
Does it behave as theory says the construct should behave?


Criterion validity
Does it correspond to an appropriate external benchmark or criterion?



Reliability is usually necessary for validity, but it is not sufficient (Bernard and Wutich 2027).
A perfectly repeatable instrument can measure the wrong thing.

Archaeological example
Suppose two analysts achieve near-perfect agreement when counting a particular grave-good type.
That result supports interobserver reliability for the count.
It does not by itself establish that:

the grave-good type measures social status;
the count captures the full domain of status;
the proposed social categories are culturally meaningful; or
status caused any observed difference in diet or mobility.

Those are validity and design questions.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Actual research is iterative
Textbooks often present a clean sequence:

topic → literature → hypothesis → design → data → analysis → publication

Real research rarely behaves that way.
Field obstacles, equipment failures, community dynamics, unexpected findings, new literature, and analytical surprises can force researchers to:

revise protocols;
redefine variables;
refine questions;
collect additional data; or
re-analyze existing data.

Bernard and Wutich describe the real research process as messier than its final published account (Bernard and Wutich 2027). Booth and colleagues make the same point: experienced research often zigzags, doubles back, and changes direction as the problem and evidence become clearer (Booth et al. 2024).






NoteIteration is not the same as improvisation without documentation



Changing a protocol can be good research.
Changing it silently is not.
When the design evolves, record what changed, why it changed, and which observations were produced under which version of the procedure.


This is one reason version control and scripted analysis matter. Marwick emphasizes that commit histories can preserve decision points and analytical changes rather than leaving a pile of ambiguously named files (Marwick 2017).

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: A research question must be doable
text:
A research question must be doable
A compelling topic is not enough.
Before beginning a study, ask whether the question is feasible.







Feasibility dimension
Question




Sustained interest
Can this question sustain serious work?


Testability
Can observable evidence address it?


Time
Can the work be completed within the available period?


Resources
Are the required equipment, funding, skills, and personnel available?


Access
Can the relevant population, archive, collection, or site be reached?



Bernard and Wutich treat feasibility as part of preparing research, not as an administrative issue added after the intellectual design (Bernard and Wutich 2027).
Ethics cuts across all five dimensions. A technically feasible study may still be inappropriate if it imposes unacceptable risk or violates obligations to participants, communities, collections, or cultural heritage.
Booth and colleagues add another useful question:

So what?

A research problem should matter to an audience beyond the fact that the researcher happens to be interested in it (Booth et al. 2024).

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Five classes of social variables
The lecture organizes social variables into five broad classes adapted from Bernard and Wutich (Bernard and Wutich 2027).








Variable class
What it concerns
Examples




Internal states
thoughts, values, beliefs, perceptions, distress
political attitudes, identity, confidence


External states
characteristics and conditions
age, economy, health, environment


Reported behavior
what people say they do
reported diet, self-reported attendance


Observed behavior
directly witnessed action
interaction, movement, task performance


Artifacts & environment
material, biological, spatial, or ecological traces
artifacts, biomarkers, settlement patterns



The distinction matters because each class raises different validity problems.
For example:

reported behavior can differ from observed behavior;
internal states require indicators rather than direct observation;
artifacts and biomarkers survive through formation processes and analytical transformations;
external states may appear straightforward but still depend on definitions and classification.

Archaeology relies heavily on the fifth class, but archaeological inference often seeks conclusions about the other four. That is why proxy reasoning and construct validity are so important.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Studies can be classified by X and Y variable types
text:
Studies can be classified by X and Y variable types
A research question can also be inspected by asking what kind of independent variable (X) is being related to what kind of dependent variable (Y).
The lecture uses a matrix to encourage systematic question generation.









Dependent variable (Y)

External-state X
Behavior / artifact X

The cell numbers are not statistical categories. They are prompts for thinking.
For example:

external state → internal state: How does household insecurity relate to perceived well-being?
internal state → reported behavior: How do beliefs relate to reported practice?
environment → observed behavior: How does distance to water affect observed movement?
external state → artifact/environment: How does settlement location relate to material distributions?


Take one research topic you care about.

Identify a plausible (X).
Identify a plausible (Y).
Classify each variable.
Explain why theory assigns those roles.
State one rival causal direction.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Separate the nature of the data from the method of analysis
text:
Separate the nature of the data from the method of analysis
A persistent mistake is to treat “qualitative” and “quantitative” as mutually exclusive research paradigms.
The lecture instead separates two questions:

What is the form of the data?
What is the method of analysis?

Bernard and Wutich emphasize that qualitative data can be analyzed quantitatively and numerical data can require qualitative interpretation (Bernard and Wutich 2027). Pelto documents a long history of ethnographic projects combining multiple forms of evidence rather than treating mixed methods as a recent invention (Pelto 2017).
A useful 2 × 2 matrix is:









Qualitative data
Quantitative data




Qualitative analysis
interpretive text, ethnography, discourse, narrative
interpreting meaning in modeled or clustered numerical results


Quantitative analysis
coding words/images into counts, free-list or content analysis
regression, ANOVA, statistical modeling



The point is not that every project must occupy all four cells. The point is that data form and analytical logic can cross.






ImportantNumbers do not automatically make a study scientific



A poorly defined variable does not become valid because it is numeric.
A careful qualitative observation does not become unscientific because it is expressed in words.
The scientific issue is whether the evidence, measurement, and reasoning are appropriate to the question.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Integration can make emic knowledge measurable
text:
Integration can make emic knowledge measurable
Emic concepts are defined in terms meaningful to members of the community being studied.
Cultural-domain methods can begin with community-generated categories and then develop structured measurements.
For example:

Free lists identify items people themselves associate with a domain.
Pile sorts reveal perceived similarities among items.
Consensus or similarity models can quantify agreement or patterned variation.

The result can remain culturally grounded while also becoming statistically analyzable.
This is an important form of validity:

The measurement dimension should not be imposed simply because it is easy to quantify; it should correspond to categories or distinctions that are meaningful for the problem and population.

Pelto’s history of mixed methods shows many ethnographic traditions in which mapping, observation, interviews, linguistic work, classification, and quantitative measures were combined in practice (Pelto 2017).

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Sequential mixed designs move in two directions
text:
Sequential mixed designs move in two directions

QUAL → QUAN
A qualitative-first sequence is useful when researchers need to learn what categories, mechanisms, or dimensions matter before constructing a structured measure.
A common logic is:

explore an unfamiliar domain → identify emic themes → build variables or survey items → test their distribution or generalizability



QUAN → QUAL
A quantitative-first sequence begins with patterns and then investigates what generated them.
A common logic is:

identify large-sample pattern → locate outliers, interactions, or unexpected groups → return to interviews/observation/context → explain mechanism

The arrow matters because the first component creates a problem that the second component is designed to address.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Research design is the structural blueprint
text:
Research design is the structural blueprint
A design should make the following chain visible:

question → objective/hypothesis → unit of analysis → sampling → measurement → data collection → analysis → conclusion

If a link is missing, the inference becomes difficult to defend.
This is why selecting a statistical technique at the end is not enough. Analysis is only one component of design (Bernard and Wutich 2027).

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Exploratory and confirmatory designs form a continuum
text:
Exploratory and confirmatory designs form a continuum
Exploratory research tends to be:

open-ended;
more inductive;
oriented toward discovery;
useful for identifying emic categories and mechanisms; and
important when relatively little is known.

Confirmatory research tends to be:

structured;
more deductive;
guided by specific hypotheses; and
oriented toward evaluating expected relationships.

Bernard and Wutich stress that the two are best understood as a continuum rather than a rigid division (Bernard and Wutich 2027).
Strong research often moves:

discovery → formulation → testing → unexpected result → renewed exploration

rather than remaining permanently at one pole.
This is consistent with Booth and colleagues’ description of real research as iterative rather than linear (Booth et al. 2024).

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Four conditions
A correlation is not, by itself, a causal explanation.
The lecture identifies four conditions normally required for a causal argument:

Covariation — (X) and (Y) vary together.
Nonspuriousness — the relationship is not produced by a third variable (Z).
Temporal precedence — the presumed cause (X) occurs before (Y).
Mechanism — a theory explains how (X) could produce (Y).

Bernard and Wutich organize causal reasoning around the same four conditions (Bernard and Wutich 2027).

Covariation
If (X) does not vary with (Y), there is little basis for claiming that (X) explains variation in (Y).
But the strength of association alone does not establish causality.


Nonspuriousness
A third variable may generate the observed relationship.
The classic logic is:
[ X Z Y ]
If (Z) causes both (X) and (Y), the observed (X)-(Y) association may be misleading.


Temporal precedence
A cause must precede its effect.
Cross-sectional data often make time order difficult to establish. Longitudinal or historical evidence may strengthen temporal reasoning.


Mechanism
Even after establishing association, nonspuriousness, and temporal order, researchers need a plausible process explaining how the cause produces the effect.
Theory is therefore part of causal inference, not decoration added after the statistics.

Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Collect at the lowest useful unit
text:
Collect at the lowest useful unit
Bernard and Wutich recommend collecting data at the lowest possible unit of analysis because fine-grained observations can be aggregated upward, whereas aggregate data usually cannot be disaggregated back into their original components (Bernard and Wutich 2027).
This principle has a direct parallel in archaeological data publication. Reiter and colleagues recommend preserving primary, non-amalgamated data and original phase associations even when later analysis combines them into broader periods (Reiter et al. 2024).






NotePreserve granularity; aggregate analytically



If data are recorded by artifact, they can later be summarized by context, phase, site, or region.
If only a site-level total survives, artifact-level variation cannot be reconstructed.
There are exceptions involving privacy, heritage protection, sensitive locations, or ethical restrictions. Granularity should be preserved where it is scientifically useful and ethically appropriate.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
The ecological fallacy
The ecological fallacy occurs when a relationship observed among groups is incorrectly interpreted as a relationship among individuals.
Suppose regions with higher average income also have higher average university attendance.
That does not prove that the higher-income individuals within each region are the individuals attending university.
The group-level association and individual-level association are different empirical questions.
In archaeology, a similar mistake can occur when a pattern among sites, cemeteries, or assemblages is projected onto individual people or artifacts without evidence at that scale.

For each statement, identify the unit of analysis.

“Households with larger storage facilities have greater crop diversity.”
“Sites closer to obsidian sources contain higher proportions of obsidian.”
“Individuals with nonlocal isotope signatures receive different burial treatment.”
“Regions with denser settlement networks show greater ceramic standardization.”

Then ask: What lower-level data would have to exist before each claim could be tested?

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
text:
Action research
Action research goes further by linking inquiry to intervention.
A simplified cycle is:

identify problem → act → evaluate → revise → act again

The goal is not only to describe conditions but to work with partners to change them.
Community-based participatory research (CBPR) and Photovoice sit toward the participant-driven, action-oriented end of this design space.






NoteResearch design also distributes power



Who defines the problem?
Who decides what counts as evidence?
Who owns the data?
Who benefits from the conclusions?
These are design questions as well as ethical questions.

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Reproducibility extends operational definition into analysis
text:
Reproducibility extends operational definition into analysis
Marwick’s principles of computational reproducibility extend the Week 3 logic beyond data collection (Marwick 2017).
A transparent research pipeline should document:

data and code provenance;
scripted analytical operations;
version control; and
the computational environment.

The common principle is explicitness.
An operational definition documents how observations became data.
A script documents how data became results.
Version control documents how the analytical workflow changed.
Metadata document what variables, units, categories, and files mean.






TipThink of reproducibility as an audit trail



A defensible analysis should allow another researcher—or your future self—to trace:
concept → measure → raw observation → transformation → analysis → figure/table → interpretation

title: Week 3 — Measurement and Research Design
section: Replicability is valuable, but it is not the only criterion
text:
Replicability is valuable, but it is not the only criterion
Vaesen and Hussain caution against making replicability the universal gatekeeper of archaeological quality (Vaesen and Hussain 2026).
Their argument is especially relevant to Week 3:

high inter-analyst agreement does not automatically guarantee validity;
preservation can create genuine ambiguity;
training traditions can shape classification;
highly replicable variables may be easy to measure but weakly informative;
difficult observations may still be behaviorally meaningful; and
methods should be chosen in relation to the research problem.

Their preferred alternative is problem-driven methodological pluralism.






ImportantLet the question guide the method



Do not choose a measure because it is easy to quantify.
Do not reject a measure only because some ambiguity remains.
Ask whether the method is appropriate to the question, whether uncertainty is documented, whether conclusions are proportionate to the evidence, and whether complementary evidence can strengthen the inference.

Exercise 3 — Diagnose measurement quality

Imagine two analysts classify the same 100 lithic artifacts.
They agree on 97 artifacts, but later discover that the shared classification rule systematically combines two technologically different categories.
Answer:

Is interobserver reliability high or low?
Does high reliability establish validity?
What kind of validity problem may exist?
What additional evidence would you want?








TipCheck your work





Interobserver reliability can be high even when the shared rule is conceptually poor.
The central problem is validity: the operational categories may not represent the technological distinction the research question requires.
You would want theory, contextual evidence, alternative coding, experimental/technological observations, and perhaps comparison with other analysts or methods.

Exercise 6 — Design a mixed-methods sequence

Choose one anthropological question and design either:

Specify:

The two components should not simply coexist.
The second component should be motivated by the first, or the two should meet at a clearly specified point where evidence is integrated, compared, explained, or transformed.

Vaesen and Hussain provide a useful counterweight to simplistic calls for standardization (Vaesen and Hussain 2026).
Their central warning is that high replicability does not automatically guarantee:

title: Course Syllabus · 2026–2027 (Term 1)
text:
Course Description
This course introduces statistical thinking and quantitative analysis for archaeology and anthropology. It is designed for students with little or no prior experience in statistics or programming. Its central goal is practical: students will learn how to move from an anthropological research question to an appropriate dataset, write understandable R code, conduct an appropriate statistical analysis, visualize the data and statistical results, and make a defensible anthropological interpretation.
The course combines fundamental concepts in research design, measurement, sampling, data quality, descriptive statistics, uncertainty, statistical inference, group comparison, association, and regression with sustained hands-on work in R, RStudio, and Quarto.
Each topic will be learned through a recurring workflow:

inspect and prepare the data → describe → visualize → analyze → visualize the result → interpret

Weekly assignments use real datasets drawn from recent published research in archaeology, biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, and linguistic anthropology. The principal graded case studies were selected using four criteria:

the research question is anthropologically substantive;
the associated publication dates after 2000;
the underlying dataset is available online through a publication supplement or open research repository; and
the statistical question can be addressed transparently with methods appropriate to an introductory course.

The emphasis is not on memorizing formulas or treating software output as an answer. Students will repeatedly be asked to understand how the data were produced, write and explain their own code, choose suitable statistical procedures, produce clear figures and tables, evaluate effect size and uncertainty, and connect statistical results to archaeological or anthropological questions while recognizing assumptions and limitations.

title: Course Syllabus · 2026–2027 (Term 1)
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Demonstrate basic data, statistical, and digital literacy, including an understanding of variables, measurement scales, distributions, sampling, uncertainty, and common sources of bias.
Translate an archaeological or anthropological research question into an explicit unit of analysis, set of variables, and appropriate statistical strategy.
Write and explain introductory R code to import, inspect, clean, transform, summarize, sample, visualize, and analyze anthropological data.
Use RStudio and Quarto to organize a reproducible workflow that integrates prose, code, tables, figures, and statistical output.
Apply and interpret introductory statistical methods, including descriptive statistics, confidence intervals, permutation tests, t-tests, chi-square tests, ANOVA, correlation, and simple linear regression.
Use ggplot2 and related R tools to explore distributions and relationships and to visualize statistical results, effect sizes, uncertainty, and model fit where appropriate.
Evaluate data provenance, missingness, sampling structure, assumptions, and dependence among observations, and communicate effect size, uncertainty, and limitations rather than relying on statistical significance alone.
Distinguish between statistical result, anthropological interpretation, and causal explanation, and evaluate quantitative claims in published archaeological and anthropological research.
Use computational and generative-AI tools responsibly as aids to learning while retaining responsibility for code comprehension, statistical reasoning, verification, interpretation, and authorship.

Core Readings and Learning Resources
Students are not expected to read any textbook from cover to cover. Each teaching week will normally include at least one focused reading explaining the statistical subject or R technique, and at least one reading connected directly to the week’s archaeological or anthropological case study.
Method readings should be used actively: students are encouraged to run the R examples while reading rather than treating the books as passive background material.

Textbooks
Available online from the UBC Library:

Perkins, Mark A. 2026. Using R for Introductory Statistics in Social Sciences. Springer, Cham.
Thulin, Måns. 2025. Modern Statistics with R: From Wrangling and Exploring Data to Inference and Predictive Modelling. Chapman and Hall/CRC.
Carlson, David Lee. 2017. Quantitative Methods in Archaeology Using R. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.
Beecham, Roger. 2026. Visualization for Social Data Science. Chapman and Hall/CRC.



Case-Study Readings
Readings associated with the weekly datasets are listed in the course schedule. These readings are part of the statistical training. For each case, students should be able to identify:

the research question;
the unit of analysis;
the key variables and their measurement scales;
how the data were produced;
the analytical strategy;
the principal statistical result; and
what the evidence does and does not justify anthropologically.

title: Course Syllabus · 2026–2027 (Term 1)
text:
Software and Computational Workflow
Students will use R, RStudio Desktop, and Quarto, all of which are free. Course examples will use a deliberately small and stable set of packages, especially tidyverse/ggplot2 and packages required for specific teaching datasets or analyses.
Most practical work will follow the same six-step workflow:

Code: load the dataset, inspect its structure, select variables, and prepare the data in R.
Describe: compute relevant descriptive statistics before running an inferential procedure.
Visualize the data: use an appropriate plot to examine distributions, groups, outliers, or relationships.
Analyze: run the statistical procedure in R and extract the quantities needed for interpretation.
Visualize the result: where useful, graph group differences, uncertainty, fitted relationships, residuals, or other model results rather than presenting raw console output alone.
Interpret: explain the statistical result in relation to archaeological or anthropological research questions, including assumptions and limitations.

All graded computational work should be completed in a Quarto (.qmd) document unless an assignment specifies otherwise. A submission should contain only the R output necessary to support the analysis; long unedited console dumps should be avoided.
Students should be able to re-render their document from a clean R session and explain every substantive line of code included in the submission.

section: Course Format, Assignments, and Due Dates
text:
Course Format, Assignments, and Due Dates
Class meetings combine concise explanation with substantial guided practice. In most two-class weeks, one class introduces the statistical logic and demonstrates the R workflow; the other functions primarily as a code-along/data-analysis lab in which students work with the week’s case-study dataset, create visualizations, conduct the analysis, and discuss interpretation. Weeks affected by holidays or the midterm break will be adjusted accordingly.
Weeks 2 and 3 emphasize software, data structure, research design, reproducibility, and practice with real research datasets but do not carry graded weekly assignments. The ten graded assignments are distributed in Weeks 4–9 and Weeks 11–14.
Students are expected to attend and participate regularly because debugging, interpretation, and statistical judgment are learned through practice. Attendance and participation account for 20% of the final grade. Absences covered by an approved academic concession, accommodation, or other recognized circumstance will be handled in accordance with UBC policy. Students who anticipate or experience an extended absence should contact the instructor as early as possible.

Weekly Assignments — 50%
There are ten graded assignments, each worth 5%, for a total of 50% of the final grade.
Each assignment asks students to submit four connected products:

working and understandable R code;
an appropriate statistical analysis;
one or more purposeful visualizations; and
a concise written interpretation tied to the anthropological research question.

Students may discuss code and statistical ideas with classmates during class unless instructed otherwise, but each student must understand the analysis and submit an independently written report.
Assignments are normally due one week after they are distributed. Exact dates and any necessary adjustments will be posted on Canvas.


Research Project — 30%
The research project asks students to carry an analysis from a published archaeological or anthropological study and its original data through a transparent and reproducible workflow. Unlike the weekly assignments, where datasets are curated for teaching, the project requires students to make and document more of their own analytical decisions while remaining within statistical methods appropriate to an introductory course.
The project will include the following steps:

Select a published case study from a list provided by the instructor, or propose another case with an accessible original dataset subject to approval.
Define one or more research questions that can be evaluated with the available data and methods learned in this course.
Obtain and document the dataset, identify the unit of analysis, create or revise a codebook, and prepare the data for analysis.
Write a reproducible R workflow that carries out the necessary data preparation and statistical analysis.
Produce clear visualizations of the data and, where appropriate, statistical estimates, uncertainty, or model results.
Evaluate assumptions, uncertainty, effect size, data quality, dependence, and other limitations.
Compare the statistical findings with the interpretation in the published study where appropriate. Students are not expected to reproduce advanced methods that lie outside the course; instead, they should clearly distinguish their ANTH418-level analysis from the fuller analysis in the publication.
Produce a clear Quarto report that integrates prose, code, tables, figures, results, and references.

Suitable public or course-supported data sources may include p3k14c, XRONOS, D-PLACE, Seshat, Kinbank, Cliopatria, the Comparative Archaeology Database when its relevant datasets are available, and the public repositories or journal supplements associated with the weekly case studies.
Students must verify that the chosen data are appropriate to their research question and that any dependence, repeated observations, spatial structure, or temporal structure is acknowledged.
Project outline: A 100–200 word outline identifying the case study, dataset, and proposed research question(s) is due Monday, 9 November 2026.
Final report: Approximately 10–12 pages, excluding references and data/code appendices, following the citation style of either American Anthropologist or American Antiquity. The report must be rendered to PDF from Quarto and should include enough executable R code and documentation for the analysis to be reproduced.
Submit the PDF together with the .qmd file, dataset(s), codebook/README, and any other files necessary to reproduce the analysis in a single ZIP file via Canvas by Friday, 11 December 2026.
The project will be evaluated on:

data provenance and documentation;
clarity and reproducibility of the R code;
appropriateness and accuracy of the statistical analysis;
quality of data and result visualizations;
interpretation of effect size and uncertainty;
treatment of assumptions and limitations;
quality of archaeological or anthropological interpretation;
clarity and organization; and
proper citation and attribution.

section: Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
text:
Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including large language models and systems that generate text, code, images, audio, or other content, is now part of the intellectual environment in which quantitative research and learning take place. This course therefore aims to teach students not simply whether AI can be used, but when it contributes to learning and when it interferes with it.

Guiding principle: augmentation rather than automation.

GenAI can be useful when it helps you ask a better question, clarify a statistical concept, understand an error message, debug code you have attempted, compare alternative analytical choices, test an interpretation, or identify weaknesses in reasoning or writing. It becomes counterproductive when it performs the statistical, programming, interpretive, or writing work that you are expected to learn to do yourself.

Permitted Use by Activity
Weekly assignments: GenAI may be used to clarify concepts, explain error messages, help debug code after you have attempted the task, suggest alternative plots or analysis strategies, or provide feedback on writing you have already produced. It may not replace the assigned analysis, produce an entire solution for submission, or substitute for your own interpretation of statistical output.
Research project: GenAI may assist with brainstorming, refining a research question, debugging, exploring possible analytical approaches, organizing a workflow, or providing feedback on a draft. It may not substitute for locating and evaluating scholarly sources, documenting or cleaning the data, creating the codebook, selecting and justifying methods, interpreting results, verifying references, or authoring the report.
In-class exercises or designated activities: Some activities may be AI-free when the purpose is to practice coding, interpretation, or statistical reasoning independently. Any such restriction will be stated by the instructor.
Students remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity, reproducibility, and authorship of everything they submit. You must be able to explain any R code, statistical procedure, output, figure, interpretation, or written argument included in your work.


Accuracy, Verification, and Disclosure
GenAI can produce plausible but incorrect statistical explanations, faulty R code, invented functions or packages, fabricated references, and oversimplified interpretations. Important claims must therefore be checked against original scholarly sources, course materials, R documentation, the actual dataset, and the statistical output generated by your own analysis.
GenAI output should not be treated as anthropological evidence or scholarly authority. When AI-generated material is itself quoted, reproduced, or analyzed as an object of study, its source should be identified in accordance with UBC guidance. Otherwise, permitted GenAI use should normally be disclosed through a brief AI Use Statement rather than cited as scholarship.
When GenAI materially contributes to submitted work in a context where its use is permitted, include a short statement at the end of the assignment or project identifying the tool, what it was used for, and how its suggestions were checked or revised. Full chat transcripts are not normally required, but students should retain relevant prompts and drafts in case clarification of the work process is needed.

Example AI Use Statement:
“I used [tool] to help interpret two R error messages and to suggest alternative ways to code a plot. I checked the suggested code against the course dataset and R documentation, revised it, and independently interpreted the final output.”

Undisclosed or unauthorized use of GenAI that substitutes for work a student is expected to perform may constitute academic misconduct.


Privacy, Access, and Instructor Use
Do not upload confidential information, restricted archaeological or anthropological data, culturally sensitive material, unpublished work belonging to others, student work, or any other information you are not authorized to share with a commercial GenAI system. Exercise similar caution with copyrighted books, articles, lecture slides, datasets, or other course materials.
No student is required to purchase a paid AI subscription for this course. All required coursework can be completed using course resources, R/RStudio, documentation, readings, office hours, and other permitted forms of assistance.
The instructor may use GenAI as a support tool in preparing teaching materials or routine course administration while remaining responsible for the accuracy, appropriateness, and academic judgment of all course content. Student work will not be submitted to external GenAI systems for assessment or analysis unless the system and use have been approved under applicable UBC privacy requirements. Final grading and substantive evaluation remain the responsibility of the instructor.
AI-detection software will not, by itself, be treated as sufficient evidence of academic misconduct. Questions about authorship or AI use may instead be addressed by discussing a student’s sources, reasoning, code, drafts, prompts where relevant, and analytical process.
If you are uncertain whether a particular use of GenAI is permitted, ask the instructor before submitting the work.
Please read UBC’s guidelines of Learning With GenAI.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Overview
This week is about learning a workflow, not memorizing commands.
R is the language we will use to work with data. RStudio is the environment in which we will organize and run that work. Quarto is the document system that brings prose, R code, results, tables, figures, and citations together in a reproducible report (Tierney 2025).
By the end of the week, you should be able to open an RStudio project, understand the basic structure of an R command, create and inspect R objects, import a CSV file, use a small set of tidyverse verbs, create a first ggplot2 figure, and render a Quarto document from a clean R session.






NoteThe Week 2 principle



Do not separate “doing the analysis” from “documenting the analysis.”
In ANTH418, the code that produces a result should live beside the explanation of what the result means.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Before class: install the software
ANTH418 assumes no previous programming experience. Before beginning the exercises below, make sure that R and RStudio are installed and working on your computer.
The three names can be confusing at first:

R is the language that performs the computation. RStudio is the application in which we will write and organize most of our R work. Quarto turns our code, results, figures, and writing into a reproducible document.


Step 1 — Install R
Download R from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN):
https://cran.r-project.org/
Choose the installer for your operating system:

macOS: choose Download R for macOS and install the current release appropriate for your Mac;
Windows: choose Download R for Windows → base → the current release; or
Linux: follow the instructions for your distribution.

Use the standard/default installation options unless you have a specific reason to change them.






NoteR must be installed before RStudio



RStudio does not replace R. It provides an easier environment for working with R, but it still needs an R installation on your computer.




Step 2 — Install RStudio Desktop
Download the free RStudio Desktop from Posit:
https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
Install the current stable release for your operating system.
On first launch, RStudio should normally find your R installation automatically.
Current versions of RStudio include integrated support for Quarto and bundle a stable Quarto release. For most ANTH418 students, installing current R and current RStudio is therefore enough to begin working with .qmd files.


Step 3 — Check Quarto
After installing RStudio, open it and choose the Terminal tab. Run:
quarto --version
You should see a version number.
Then run:
quarto check
This checks whether Quarto can find the software it needs, including R and the Knitr execution engine.






TipDo I need to install Quarto separately?



Usually no if you have installed a current release of RStudio, because RStudio bundles Quarto.
If quarto --version does not work, or if you need a newer standalone Quarto release, install it from:
https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/
After installation, restart RStudio and run quarto --version again.




Step 4 — Install the R packages used in ANTH418
Packages extend what R can do. For the first part of the course, the main package collection we need is the tidyverse.
In the R Console, run:
install.packages("tidyverse")
You normally install a package only once on a computer.
Then test that it loads:
library(tidyverse)
If the command finishes without an error, the package is available.






ImportantConsole or Terminal?



RStudio contains both, but they serve different purposes.

Use the R Console for R commands such as install.packages() and library().
Use the Terminal for system commands such as quarto --version and quarto check.

We will use both during the course.




Step 5 — Verify the complete setup
In the R Console, run:
R.version.string
1 + 1
library(tidyverse)
You should see your R version, the result 2, and no error when the tidyverse loads.
In the Terminal, run:
quarto --version
If those checks work, you have the basic ANTH418 computational environment.


Step 6 — Make a tiny Quarto test document
In RStudio choose:
File → New File → Quarto Document…
Choose HTML and create the document. Replace its body with:
## My first R calculation


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
2 + 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4
```


:::
:::
Save the file as something like:
quarto_test.qmd
Then click Render.
If an HTML page appears showing both the code and the result 4, then R, RStudio, Knitr, and Quarto are communicating correctly.






NoteYou do not need every optional tool



quarto check may report that tools such as TinyTeX, Jupyter, or Julia are not installed. That is fine for the R-based HTML work in ANTH418.
Do not install extra software simply to make every optional check appear as installed.




If installation fails
Do not spend hours troubleshooting alone. Record:

your operating system;
the exact error message;
what you were trying to install or run; and
a screenshot if useful.

Bring that information to class or office hours. Error messages are evidence: copy them exactly rather than paraphrasing them.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
R, RStudio, and Quarto

R
R is a programming language and statistical computing environment.
When you write
mean(c(4, 7, 9))
R evaluates the instruction and returns a result.
R is where the computation happens.


RStudio
RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE). It gives you a convenient place to work with R:

the Source pane for scripts and Quarto documents;
the Console for commands and output;
the Environment pane for objects currently in memory;
the Files / Plots / Packages / Help panes for navigating the project and inspecting results; and
project tools that help keep files, code, and working directories organized.

An RStudio Project is especially important because it gives a project a stable root directory. Project-based organization prevents many file-path problems and makes analyses more portable (Tierney 2025).


Quarto
Quarto is a scientific and technical publishing system.
A Quarto document can contain:

Markdown prose;
executable R code;
tables;
figures;
equations;
citations; and
cross-references.

The .qmd source is the document you edit. Rendering turns it into an output such as HTML, PDF, or Word.






TipA useful mental model



R computes. RStudio organizes. Quarto communicates reproducibly.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Projects and file paths
A reproducible analysis should not depend on a path that only exists on your own computer.
Avoid code such as:
# Do not write paths like this in course work:
read_csv("/Users/yourname/Desktop/my-course/data/file.csv")
and avoid beginning an analysis with:
setwd("/Users/yourname/some/very/specific/location")
Instead, open the relevant RStudio Project and work with relative paths:
read_csv("data/file.csv")
This is one of the workflow practices emphasized in Quarto for Scientists: keep the files for one project together and let the project establish a stable starting point for your analysis (Tierney 2025).

Inspect your current project
Run these commands in the Console:

getwd()
list.files()
file.exists("data")


Your turn — read a file path.
In the path data/knipper2020_humans.csv:

What is the directory?
What is the file?
Is the path absolute or relative?
Why is this path more portable than one beginning with /Users/...?

Vectors and data types
A vector contains multiple values of the same basic type. Thulin introduces vectors and data frames as fundamental structures for storing observations in R (Thulin 2025).

WarningNA is not zero

This distinction will become a major analytical issue in Week 6.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Functions
A function is a reusable set of instructions. A function usually takes one or more inputs—called arguments—and returns a result. This function-centered way of working is fundamental to R (Perkins 2026; Thulin 2025).

isotope_values <- c(10.2, 11.4, 9.8, 12.1)

mean(isotope_values)

[1] 10.875

min(isotope_values)

[1] 9.8

max(isotope_values)

[1] 12.1

length(isotope_values)

[1] 4


The basic pattern is:
function_name(argument)
Functions can have additional arguments:

values_with_missing <- c(10.2, 11.4, NA, 12.1)

mean(values_with_missing)

[1] NA

mean(values_with_missing, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 11.23333



Ask R for help
Use ? or help():

?mean
help(mean)
?read_csv







TipDo not try to memorize every function



Professional R users repeatedly consult documentation. The goal is to understand what you want to do, recognize the relevant function, read its arguments, and verify its behavior.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto

Data frames and tibbles
Most ANTH418 datasets will be rectangular tables:

rows represent observations;
columns represent variables.

In R, these are stored as data frames. Tidyverse packages commonly use a modern data-frame format called a tibble.

  site = c("La Bastida", "La Bastida", "Gatas"),
  d15n = c(10.4, 11.7, 9.9)
)

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Overview
Week 3 asked how concepts become variables and how research design limits inference. Week 4 asks what to do once a defensible numerical variable has been measured:

How can we describe a distribution without losing the pattern that matters?

Raw observations rarely explain themselves. A list of isotope values, ceramic dimensions, fossil measurements, or survey scores may contain important structure, but that structure is difficult to see until the observations are organized, visualized, and summarized. The Week 4 lecture therefore begins with a simple sequence:
raw observations → summary numbers → empirical pattern → interpretation
Descriptive statistics do not explain why a pattern exists. They make the empirical pattern visible enough that an explanation can later be evaluated.
Two questions organize the entire week:

Central tendency: Where is the distribution centered? What value is typical?
Dispersion / variability: How widely are observations spread around that center?

A center without a measure of spread is incomplete. Two archaeological samples can have the same mean and radically different internal variation. Conversely, two samples can have different means but substantial overlap. This is why the Week 4 lecture treats central tendency and dispersion as a pair rather than as separate topics.
Carlson makes the archaeological version of the same point: the first step in analyzing new data is to look at the data, using numerical summaries, tables, and graphs to identify structure and possible errors before more elaborate analysis begins (Carlson 2017). Banning similarly treats descriptive statistics as a way to summarize both where typical values lie and how “clumped” or dispersed archaeological observations are (Banning 2020).






NoteThe Week 4 principle



Describe before explaining.
A defensible descriptive analysis tells the reader:

what was measured;
what one observation represents;
where the distribution is centered;
how much it varies;
what its shape looks like; and
which observations are unusual.

Only then should we ask why the pattern may exist.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Raw tables do not explain themselves
text:
Raw tables do not explain themselves
A dataset is a collection of observations, not an interpretation.
Carlson emphasizes that archaeological datasets are commonly organized as rectangular tables in which each row represents an observation and each column represents a measurement or attribute of that observation (Carlson 2017). The meaning of a row can change from dataset to dataset: one row might be a survey grid square, a site, a grave, a ceramic sherd, a stone flake, or a human individual.
That means the first questions are not mathematical:

What does one row represent? What does each column represent? How was each variable measured?

Only after those questions are answered do numerical summaries become meaningful.






ImportantA statistic summarizes observations; it does not replace them



Reducing 69 isotope measurements to a mean is useful because it compresses information.
But compression always loses detail.
The goal is therefore not to find one “best number” and discard the distribution. The goal is to combine a small set of summaries with appropriate visualizations so that the center, spread, shape, and unusual observations remain visible.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: A mean can be calculable and meaningless
text:
A mean can be calculable and meaningless
Suppose an artifact-material variable is coded:
Ceramic = 1
Lithic  = 2
Bone    = 3
R can calculate the arithmetic mean of those numbers.
But a “mean artifact material” of 2.13 has no archaeological interpretation because the numbers are merely labels. The distance from ceramic to lithic is not a measured quantitative interval.






NoteNumeric storage is not quantitative meaning



A variable can be stored as numbers in R and still be nominal.
Always distinguish:

how R stores the column, from
what the measurements mean.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: What scale are δ13C and δ15N?
text:
What scale are δ13C and δ15N?
For Assignment 1, human bone-collagen (^{13}) and (^{15}) values are best treated as interval-like measurements for descriptive purposes.
Differences between values are meaningful, but (0‰) is a reference point relative to an isotope standard—not a true absence of carbon or nitrogen isotope composition. Therefore:

means and medians are meaningful;
SD, variance, IQR, and range are meaningful;
ratios such as “twice the δ15N value” are not meaningful; and
CV is not appropriate for the delta values in Assignment 1.







ImportantWhy this matters



Week 4 introduces the coefficient of variation because it is important in anthropology.
But learning a statistic does not mean using it everywhere.
Assignment 1 requires SD, IQR, minimum, maximum, and range—not CV—because the measurement scale and research question do not justify CV for these delta isotope values.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Central tendency summarizes “typical”
A measure of central tendency reduces a distribution to a value intended to represent its center.
The three classical centers are:








Measure
Definition
Particularly useful when




Mode
most frequently occurring value/category
nominal data; discrete peaks; multimodality


Median
50th percentile
ordinal data; skewed data; outliers


Mean
arithmetic average
approximately symmetric interval/ratio data


Trimmed mean
mean after removing equal percentages from both tails
continuous data with influential extremes



Choosing a center is a methodological decision, not a mechanical habit.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: The mode: the most frequent value
text:
The mode: the most frequent value
The mode is the value or category occurring most often.
For categorical variables it may be the only meaningful measure of central tendency.
For continuous archaeological measurements, an exact numerical mode is often less useful because repeated values may depend on measurement precision and rounding. However, modal peaks in a frequency distribution can be archaeologically informative.
The lecture uses standardized stone weights from Mohenjo-Daro as an example: repeated peaks can reveal patterned size classes rather than one smooth continuous distribution.

Unimodal, bimodal, and multimodal
A distribution can have:

one dominant peak — unimodal;
two dominant peaks — bimodal; or
several peaks — multimodal.

Multiple peaks may reflect real subgroups, different production conventions, different populations, or a mixture of processes. They may also arise from small samples or arbitrary histogram bins.






WarningA histogram peak is not automatically a statistical mode



Changing histogram bin width can change the apparent number and location of peaks.
When multimodality matters substantively, inspect the raw values and test whether the apparent structure is robust to reasonable choices of binning.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The median: the positional center
The median is the middle value after observations are ordered.

50% of observations lie at or below it.
50% lie at or above it.

For an odd number of observations, the median is the middle observation.
For an even number, it is conventionally the average of the two middle observations.
The important property is resistance: the median depends on order, not on how far extreme observations lie from the middle.

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8)
x_extreme <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 80)

tibble(
  dataset = c("Original", "One extreme value"),
  mean = c(mean(x), mean(x_extreme)),
  median = c(median(x), median(x_extreme))
)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  dataset            mean median
  <chr>             <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Original            6        7
2 One extreme value  20.4      7


The extreme value moves the mean much more than the median.
Dressler uses this contrast to show why mean, median, and mode can converge in an approximately symmetric distribution but diverge when a distribution has a long tail (Dressler 2015).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: The arithmetic mean: the balance point
text:
The arithmetic mean: the balance point
For a sample of (n) observations:
[ {x} = ]
The mean uses every observation.
It can be understood as the distribution’s balance point or center of gravity. If each deviation from the mean is calculated,
[ x_i - {x}, ]
then the deviations sum to zero:
[ _{i=1}^{n}(x_i-{x})=0. ]
This balance property makes the mean fundamental to variance, standard deviation, regression, ANOVA, and many later statistical methods.
Pivitera describes the mean as a balance point rather than necessarily the literal middle observation (Privitera 2024). Dressler similarly presents the mean as a compact model or “best guess” for a value drawn from a roughly symmetric distribution (Dressler 2015).






WarningThe mean is efficient but not resistant



Because every observation contributes to the mean, an extreme observation can pull the balance point toward the tail.
That sensitivity is not a defect to be hidden. It is information about the distribution that should be examined.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: The trimmed mean: a robust compromise
text:
The trimmed mean: a robust compromise
A trimmed mean removes the same proportion of the lowest and highest observations before calculating the mean.
Common trims include 5%, 10%, or 20%.
In R:

x_extreme <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 80)

mean(x_extreme)

[1] 15.2

mean(x_extreme, trim = 0.10)

[1] 8.625

median(x_extreme)

[1] 8.5


Banning notes that trimmed means can be useful for skewed archaeological distributions or samples containing suspected extremes because they retain much of the data while reducing tail influence (Banning 2020).
A trimmed mean is not required for Assignment 1, but it helps clarify why “center” is not one universal concept.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Why dispersion matters
Suppose two assemblages both have mean artifact length = 50 mm.
One contains measurements tightly concentrated between 48 and 52 mm.
The other ranges from 20 to 80 mm.
The means are identical, but the archaeological patterns are not.
Pivitera emphasizes that variability widens the lens from the center to the structure of the entire distribution (Privitera 2024). Dressler puts the same idea in practical terms: after using a mean as a guess, the next question is how wrong that guess is likely to be (Dressler 2015).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The range
The range is:
[ =-. ]
It is easy to understand, but it depends on only two observations.

x <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14)
x_outlier <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 100)

c(
  range_original = max(x) - min(x),
  range_with_outlier = max(x_outlier) - min(x_outlier)
)

    range_original range_with_outlier 
                 4                 90 


The range is therefore fragile:

it is highly sensitive to extreme observations;
it tends to increase as sample size increases; and
it says nothing about how observations are distributed between the minimum and maximum.

Banning makes the archaeological implication explicit: because the range depends only on the two extremes, it is usually a poor stand-alone description of variability (Banning 2020).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Percentiles and quartiles
A percentile is the value below which a specified percentage of observations lies.
Quartiles divide an ordered distribution into four parts:

(Q_1): 25th percentile;
(Q_2): 50th percentile = median;
(Q_3): 75th percentile.

Each interval between successive quartile boundaries contains roughly one quarter of the observations.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Interquartile range (IQR)
The interquartile range is:
[ IQR = Q_3 - Q_1. ]
It describes the width of the middle 50% of a distribution.
Because it ignores the most extreme quarter at each end, it is much less sensitive to outliers than the total range.
Median + IQR therefore form a natural descriptive pair.

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12)

quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75))

25% 50% 75% 
  7   8  10 

IQR(x)

[1] 3


Gonick and Smith’s illustrated treatment makes the same geometry visible: the box in a boxplot runs from (Q_1) to (Q_3), with the median drawn inside (Gonick and Smith 2019).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Boxplots: a compact display of center and spread

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Why simple deviations cannot measure total spread
text:
Why simple deviations cannot measure total spread
The deviation of an observation from the sample mean is:
[ d_i = x_i-{x}. ]
But positive and negative deviations cancel:
[ d_i = 0. ]
So we square them.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Sample variance
For a sample:
[ s^2 = . ]
Variance is the average squared distance around the mean, with the sample correction (n-1).
The numerator,
[ (x_i-{x})^2, ]
is called the sum of squares.
Perkins walks through this logic by subtracting the mean from each value, squaring the deviations, summing them, dividing by (n-1), and then taking the square root to obtain SD (Perkins 2026).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Why (n-1)?
If the data are treated as a sample used to estimate population variability, dividing by (n) tends to underestimate the population variance.
Using (n-1) is the familiar Bessel correction.
R’s:
var(x)
sd(x)
use the sample formulas with (n-1).
For Assignment 1, that is exactly what students should use.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Standard deviation
The standard deviation is:
[ s=. ]
Variance has squared units:

mm²;
g²;
‰².

Taking the square root returns the result to the original measurement units.
That is why SD is generally easier to interpret than variance.
Dressler emphasizes this return to the original metric: the squaring needed to construct variance makes the units difficult to interpret, while the square root restores them (Dressler 2015).






NoteInterpret SD as spread, not as a guaranteed boundary



A larger SD means observations are, on average, more dispersed around the mean.
It does not mean every observation falls within one SD of the mean.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Median absolute deviation (MAD)
A robust alternative to SD is the median absolute deviation:
[ MAD = (|x_i-(x)|). ]
Like the median and IQR, MAD is resistant to extreme observations.
In R, note an important detail:

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 80)

# Raw median absolute deviation from the median:
mad(x, constant = 1)

[1] 2

# R's default is scaled to estimate SD under normality:
mad(x)

[1] 2.9652


MAD is not required for Assignment 1, but it provides a useful comparison when distributions are strongly skewed or contain influential extremes.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Coefficient of variation (CV)
For an appropriate ratio-scale variable:
[ CV=%. ]
CV expresses variability relative to the magnitude of the mean.
This matters when absolute SD naturally increases with body size or scale.

Bioanthropological application
Plavcan shows why relative variability matters in studies of living primates and fossil hominins. An SD measured in grams or millimeters will naturally be larger for a large-bodied species than for a small-bodied species, even if their relative variability is similar (Plavcan 2012).
The CV places variation on a relative scale.
Plavcan’s comparative data also show why simple universal cutoffs are dangerous: within-sex variation differs by trait. Many craniofacial dimensions in living primates have CVs below 10%, while body-mass CVs can be around 12–15%; fossil interpretation must also consider geography, time, sex, taxonomy, sample quality, and trait choice (Plavcan 2012).






WarningCV is not a universal standardization detector



The lecture uses CV to illustrate technological standardization and biological size variation.
A low CV can be consistent with standardized production, but it does not by itself prove specialist production.
Sampling, raw material, function, measurement protocol, temporal mixing, and the scale of the mean can all affect observed variability.




Why Assignment 1 does not use CV
Assignment 1 compares (^{13}) and (^{15}) delta values.
Because their zero points are reference points rather than true absence, a ratio such as (s/{x}) does not have the interpretation required for CV.
Use the assignment’s requested measures:

SD;
IQR;
minimum;
maximum; and
range.
