Symmetric distributions
In a reasonably symmetric unimodal distribution:
[ . ]
Mean + SD can often provide an effective compact description.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Positive / right skew
A right-skewed distribution has a long tail toward larger values.
Extreme high values pull the mean upward:
[ > ]
is a common pattern.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Negative / left skew
A left-skewed distribution has a long tail toward smaller values.
Extreme low values pull the mean downward:
[ < . ]

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Skewness is a clue, not a verdict
text:
Skewness is a clue, not a verdict
Mean–median differences can signal asymmetry, but they are not a complete diagnostic.
Always inspect the distribution itself.
Perkins’s R chapter demonstrates why: a histogram reveals tail structure and unusual observations that a table of descriptive statistics can summarize but cannot fully display (Perkins 2026).






NotePair the statistic with the picture



A useful Week 4 habit is:
histogram → boxplot → numerical summaries → interpretation
not:
mean → conclusion.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Archaeological standardization
Archaeologists can compare dispersion in:

ceramic dimensions;
projectile-point measurements;
brick sizes;
weight systems; or
other manufactured objects.

A tightly clustered distribution may be consistent with stronger standardization; a broader distribution may indicate greater heterogeneity.
But Banning’s larger methodological warning remains essential: apparent variation can also arise from measurement protocol, analyst decisions, sampling, classification, or the archaeological formation process (Banning 2020).
Thus:

variation becomes archaeological evidence only after we understand how the variation was produced.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Means can also be misleading because of measurement decisions
text:
Means can also be misleading because of measurement decisions
Banning gives an especially important archaeological example: average artifact size depends on what counts as a measurable artifact. If one analyst includes fragments down to 1 cm and another includes only pieces above 2 cm, they can obtain different means from the same underlying material (Banning 2020).
The lesson connects Week 3 to Week 4:

descriptive statistics inherit every decision built into measurement and sampling.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: El Argar, La Bastida, and Gatas
text:
El Argar, La Bastida, and Gatas
Assignment 1 is based on Knipper et al.’s study of the El Argar society of southeast Iberia, approximately 2200–1550 cal BCE (Knipper et al. 2020).
El Argar was a complex Bronze Age society characterized by:

fortified settlements;
cereal agriculture;
metallurgy;
hierarchical social organization; and
marked funerary inequality.

The study compares La Bastida and Gatas, two hilltop settlements with social, economic, and environmental differences.
Knipper and colleagues analyzed several positions in the food web:

cereals → domestic animals → humans

They measured stable carbon and nitrogen isotope composition in charred cereal grains and in animal and human bone collagen (Knipper et al. 2020).
This broader design matters because the Assignment 1 teaching file contains only the human observations.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The usable human sample
The original study sampled 75 humans:

52 from La Bastida;
23 from Gatas.

Six samples were excluded from interpretation because collagen preservation was insufficient.
The evaluable human results are therefore:

La Bastida: 48
Gatas: 21
Total: 69

These 69 observations form the Assignment 1 teaching dataset (Knipper et al. 2020).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: What δ13C and δ15N can tell us

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The crucial archaeological lesson
The human values at La Bastida are higher on average for both (^{13}) and (^{15}) than at Gatas in the original study (Knipper et al. 2020).
A tempting interpretation would be:

Higher human (^{15}) at La Bastida = more meat or dairy.

The full food-web evidence makes that inference unsafe.
Knipper et al. found differences in cereal and animal baselines as well. Their results indicate extensive rain-fed cereal cultivation with little to moderate manuring, and especially at La Bastida they found strong integration between crop production and domestic-animal feeding. When plant and animal baselines are considered, higher human isotope values do not necessarily imply different average dietary composition (Knipper et al. 2020).






ImportantAssignment 1 is intentionally narrower than the published paper



Your task is not to reproduce Knipper et al.’s complete dietary reconstruction.
Your task is to establish:

What do the observed human isotope distributions show?

Only after describing the distributions should you discuss archaeological interpretations that are consistent with the evidence.

Step 9 — Understand every column in the summary

sd
The sample standard deviation.
It is expressed in the same unit as the isotope measurement: ‰.


iqr
The width of the middle 50%.
It is resistant to the tails and pairs naturally with the median.


min, max, and range

text:
Step 11 — Compare SD with IQR
SD and IQR do not measure exactly the same thing, so do not compare their raw magnitudes as if they should be equal.
Instead ask:

Does the boxplot show a compact middle 50% but long tails?
Does the range look large relative to the IQR?
Are one or two observations influencing the SD?
Are the data reasonably symmetric so that mean + SD give a useful compact description?
Would median + IQR more faithfully represent the center and central spread?







NoteThere is no rule that you must choose only one pair



A good descriptive report can present both:

mean + SD; and
median + IQR

Step 13 — Describe first, interpret second
A strong Assignment 1 paragraph has two stages.

Stage A — Statistical description
Describe only what the human distributions show.
A useful template is:

For (^{15}), the La Bastida sample had a [higher/lower/similar] center than Gatas. The mean and median were [close/different], while the SD and IQR indicate [greater/lower/similar] variability. The histogram and boxplot show [symmetry/skew/tails/overlap/unusual observations].

Use your actual output to replace the bracketed phrases.


Stage B — Archaeological interpretation
Then explain what is consistent with the pattern while respecting the limits of the assignment.
A useful transition is:

These descriptive differences demonstrate variation in the human isotope distributions, but they do not by themselves identify the dietary or agricultural mechanism that produced it.

Then bring in Knipper et al.’s wider plant–animal–human evidence (Knipper et al. 2020).

section: Step 14 — Answer the assignment’s four interpretive questions
text:
Step 14 — Answer the assignment’s four interpretive questions

1. What is the unit of analysis?
One sampled human individual.


2. What descriptive statistical result matters most?
There is no single answer supplied in advance.
Choose the result that most clearly characterizes the important empirical pattern and justify the choice using the visualizations and summary statistics.


3. What archaeological or anthropological interpretation is consistent with the distributions?
Your interpretation should be cautious and contextual.
The human distributions can be discussed in relation to the broader El Argar food-web study, but the Assignment 1 data alone do not reconstruct the entire food system.


4. What claim do these descriptive data alone not support?
Examples of claims that would require additional evidence include:

exact proportions of meat, dairy, barley, or other foods;
a causal claim that site status produced isotope differences;
a claim that higher (^{15}) necessarily means more animal protein;
a population-wide claim about all inhabitants of La Bastida or Gatas;
a causal claim about manuring or irrigation from the human dataset alone.

text:
Exercise 1 — Which center?

Consider:
3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 80
Without using R:

Which value will affect the mean most?
Will the median change dramatically because of the value 80?
Which center better describes a “typical” observation here?
What additional plot would you want to see before making a final decision?








TipCheck your reasoning





The value 80 strongly affects the mean but has much less influence on the median.
The median is therefore more resistant for this strongly right-tailed toy dataset.
A histogram, dot plot, or boxplot would help show whether 80 is isolated from the main body of observations.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 2 — Same mean, different spread

Compare:
a <- c(8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
b <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20)

Calculate the mean of each.
Calculate the SD of each.
What would be lost if you reported only the means?








TipCheck with R





mean(a)
mean(b)

sd(a)
sd(b)
The means are the same, but the second dataset is much more dispersed.
This is why central tendency without dispersion is incomplete.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 3 — Range versus IQR

Start with:
x <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16)
Then replace 16 with 100.
Compare:

range;
IQR.

Which statistic changes more, and why?







TipCheck with R





x1 <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16)
x2 <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 100)

max(x1) - min(x1)
max(x2) - min(x2)

IQR(x1)
IQR(x2)
The range depends directly on the extreme values, whereas the IQR focuses on the middle 50%.

text:
Exercise 5 — Choose the summary pair

For each hypothetical distribution, choose the most informative primary pair:

mean + SD, or
median + IQR.


A
Symmetric, unimodal, no influential extremes.


B
Strong right skew with several high values.


C
Ordinal preservation scores: poor / fair / good / excellent.
Explain your choices.








TipCheck your reasoning






A: mean + SD is usually efficient and interpretable.
B: median + IQR is more resistant, though reporting both pairs can reveal the effect of the tail.
C: median + IQR is compatible with ordered categories; an arithmetic mean assumes quantitative intervals not supplied by the labels.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 6 — Is CV appropriate?

Would CV be appropriate for:

femoral-head diameter in mm?
body mass in kg?
(^{15}) reported in ‰ relative to a standard?
temperature in °C?

Explain the measurement-scale reason for each answer.







TipCheck your reasoning





CV requires a ratio scale with a meaningful nonzero mean.
It is defensible for femoral-head diameter and body mass.
It is not appropriate for delta isotope values or Celsius temperature because their zero points are reference points rather than true absence.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 7 — Separate description from explanation

Rewrite this sentence so that statistical description and archaeological explanation are separated:

“La Bastida people ate more meat because their mean δ15N is higher.”

Your revision should contain:

one descriptive sentence; and
one cautious interpretive sentence.








TipOne defensible structure





A stronger structure is:

The La Bastida human sample has higher δ15N values on average than the Gatas sample.

Then:

This descriptive difference does not by itself demonstrate greater meat consumption, because isotope baselines also vary across crops and animals; the wider food-web evidence is needed to evaluate the mechanism.

The exact wording should reflect your own Assignment 1 results and reading of Knipper et al. (Knipper et al. 2020).

Error 6 — Treating ±2 SD as a confidence interval for the mean

The empirical rule concerns the expected spread of observations under an approximately normal distribution.

Error 9 — Forgetting unequal sample sizes
La Bastida has 48 observations; Gatas has 21.
A smaller sample often produces a rougher-looking histogram and less stable extremes.
That does not make the smaller sample invalid, but it should temper visual interpretation.
